strengths: Clear motivation with empirical evidence (Figure 1) that better unmasking policies exist beyond max-confidence heuristics
Comprehensive theoretical framework with Theorem 2 providing KL divergence tightening guarantees and multiple reference policy realizations with detailed derivations
Memory-efficient training approach (134M policy model vs 8B base model) enabling practical deployment with frozen MDM
Consistent empirical improvements across all four benchmarks with strong gains on SUDOKU (11.2% over max-confidence)
Extensive supplementary material with detailed proofs, algorithms (Algorithm 2), and implementation specifics supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Theorem 1 is directly restated from Mroueh (2025); only Theorem 2 is novel but relatively straightforward—intuitively, improving expected reward should yield distributions closer to the data. Core idea of applying GRPO to MDM components duplicates Huang et al. (2025, DCOLT) and Zhao et al. (2025, diffu-GRPO)

Weak theoretical contributions: Theorem 2 assumes unrealistic ideal MDM with LMDM(θ*) = 0, strong support condition supp(pgref(·|q)) ⊇ supp(pθ*(·|q)), lacks tightness analysis, and proof heavily depends on Lemma 1 from prior work

Unfair experimental comparisons: Deterministic max-confidence baseline vs stochastic learned policy; different reference policies used per dataset (max-confidence for SUDOKU/ZEBRA, Top-K for GSM8K/MATH500) without justification; learned policy receives GRPO training signal while baselines do not; no ablation testing if max-confidence would improve under same training regime

Contradictory framing: Title claims to go 'beyond explicit reference policies' but entire framework requires KL-regularized reference policy as core component; more accurately describes using reference policies more effectively, not transcending them

Limited experimental scope: Single base model (LLaDA-8B) evaluated; generalization to other MDMs undemonstrated; no statistical significance testing, error bars, or confidence intervals; modest improvements on realistic benchmarks (ZEBRA: 2.5 pp, MATH500: 1.2 pp; only SUDOKU strong at 11.2 pp)

Missing critical comparisons and ablations: No direct comparison with DCOLT despite high relevance; no ablation on regularization coefficient β; no sensitivity analysis for policy architecture; no investigation of whether max-confidence benefits equally from GRPO; Figure 4 ablation shows regularization prevents collapse but improvements remain marginal

Inconsistent experimental design across datasets: Post-hoc justification ('strongest configuration depends on task') for using different reference realizations undermines generality; appears to cherry-pick best-performing reference per benchmark

Insufficient analysis of learned behavior: No visualization, interpretation, or systematic analysis of what policies learn; unclear if improvements stem from systematic orderings or spurious patterns; limited mechanistic understanding

Methodological concerns: Proposition 1 assumes 'ϕ ≈ ϕold' for gradient alignment but GRPO may produce larger updates; impact of StopGrad on trajectory probability gradients unaddressed; advantage standardization uses old policy statistics potentially introducing bias

Presentation and reproducibility gaps: Dense notation obscures key insights; Example 1 oversimplified; computational training cost not quantified; code availability not mentioned despite claimed emphasis on reproducibility; improvements modest (1-2%) relative to claimed training overhead

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear evidence that better unmasking trajectories exist beyond max-confidence heuristics (Figure 1)

Strong theoretical contributions: Theorem 1 proves convergence to improved performance; Theorem 2 proves optimized policy generates samples closer to data distribution; rigorous proofs with careful handling of measure-theoretic subtleties
Practical efficiency: Memory-efficient training with frozen base MDM (134M vs 8B), compatible with existing improvements like diffu-GRPO
Comprehensive experimental validation across diverse benchmarks (SUDOKU, ZEBRA, GSM8K, MATH500) with thorough ablations showing value of regularization
Clear improvements on structured reasoning: SUDOKU 70.5%→81.7% (+11.2%), ZEBRA 33.7%→36.2% (+2.5%), with qualitative analysis showing learned policy avoids constraint-propagation failures
Multiple reference policy realizations (max-confidence, softmax, Top-K) provide flexibility; detailed algorithms enable reproducibility
Technical soundness: Rigorous proofs adapted to finite-horizon sparse-reward MDPs with careful treatment of support assumptions and absolute continuity
weaknesses: Limited improvements on most important benchmarks: GSM8K +1.9%, MATH500 +1.2%; gains most impressive on structured puzzles, raising questions about generalization to open-ended reasoning

Theory-practice gap: Theorem 2 assumes ideal MDM with zero training loss and binary rewards, but practice uses incomplete MDMs with dense rewards (binary signal + auxiliary log-probabilities); modifications are somewhat ad-hoc
Reference policy selection requires task-specific tuning: max-confidence optimal for SUDOKU, Top-K for GSM8K, but no principled method provided for new tasks
Limited generalization analysis: All experiments train separate policies per dataset; Appendix D.2's exploration of preference rewards on natural language is preliminary with only two datasets
Incomplete comparison with related work: DCOLT (concurrent work on learned policies) is only compared indirectly in Figure 3; no head-to-head evaluation on same benchmarks
Computational cost during training not fully analyzed: Wall-clock time and sample complexity not reported; unclear if training cost is justified relative to using max-confidence with more iterations
Limited analysis of what patterns the policy learns: SUDOKU examples show qualitative success but don't reveal structural insights that could inform future heuristics
Assumption of frozen MDM limits potential improvements: Joint optimization approaches (like DCOLT) could yield better results but add computational cost; trade-off not quantified empirically
